title: Properly applying the protective and hypertrophic properties of lower body movem
summary: NH explains that knee flexion and hip hinge always occur together, and fighting this synergy (overly upright squats, straight-leg good mornings) causes injuries. Mimicking visual cues causes other errors: pushing the butt back before descending, squatting down to the deadlift bar, and hyperextending the lockout. Proper patterns protect the body and maximise tonnage to target muscles.
claims: Movement patterns centre on a joint that activates the surrounding muscles; squats are natural
Squats are more functional than pull-ups for most people; the vertical pull is one of the least functional movements for the average person
Everyone moves on the same model; leverages change stance and technique, not the basic pattern
Pure knee flexion and pure hip hinge don't exist under load: descending far enough forces the other pattern because the body wants to use as many muscles as possible
Isolation practice doesn't replace compounds; heavier, safer compound work gives more tonnage, and lagging small muscles can be hit afterwards
Squatting with an excessively vertical torso to isolate quads invites knee injury; the knee needs hamstring engagement to stay healthy
Forcing a pure hip hinge causes lower back pain or hamstring tears because the hamstrings compensate for missing quad activation
This disqualifies straight-leg good mornings and squat variations that keep the hip from ever hinging
Don't resist the hip hinge in a squat: accompany it and limit deviation through technique
Over-resisting the hinge weakens it, until form collapses into a good-morning squat that snaps something
Don't judge form by visual cues: lower back rounding on a deadlift is a symptom of the hips shooting up and no posterior chain or thoracic extension
A proper squat starts with knee flexion; the torso angle then shifts into a hip hinge at depth and unwinds into pure knee extension on the way up
Pushing the butt back before the knees bend shifts the centre of gravity back, reducing glute/hamstring engagement and causing a good-morning squat that loads the lower back
Deadlift setup: bend the knees slightly, push the butt back and reach for the bar; don't squat down to it
Before pulling, have shoulders over the bar and some knee flexion; too much knee bend puts you behind the bar in a weird half squat
Knee flexion in a deadlift and slight hinge in a squat are cues to trigger muscles, never the main mover
A proper lockout is a neutral back with joints aligned; hyperextending and thrusting the hips is unnecessary and dangerous
Exaggerated lockouts come from lifters with soft knees faking a strong lockout, especially sumo lifters whose leg angle hides a soft lockout
Glute power develops throughout the deadlift, not at lockout; you don't need an extra hip thrust at the top
Proper movement patterns feel painless and fully activated, protect the body and give the most repeatable tonnage for hypertrophy
exercises: initiate with knee flexion, let the hip hinge come naturally, don't push butt back first
pattern synergy protects knees and back
bend knees, push butt back, reach for bar; shoulders over bar; neutral lockout without hyperextension
posterior chain loading without lumbar risk
forcing a pure hinge risks hamstrings and lower back
lockout often faked by leaning back
